batches.title: Step 1, from the five theorems to one statement

units.states: The first theorem of `Main.lean` says that a Dirichlet L-function has no zero with real part above 1/2, with the trivial character at s = 1 set aside.
Of the five theorems two are about the zeta function and three are about Dirichlet L-functions. The four after the first follow from the first.
units.read: the calls in `Main.lean` read, the two named theorems unread

units.states: The first theorem follows from `ZeroFreeAll`, which says for every primitive Dirichlet character that its L-function has no zero with real part above 1/2. The theorem `imprimitive` carries that to every Dirichlet character through the Euler factors, with the trivial character at s = 1 set aside.
`ZeroFreeAll` is proved from three premises, which the code calls `Green`, `VWin` and the existence of a record `HypsAlt`.

batches.title: Step 2, from a bound on intervals to zero-freeness

units.states: `Gm x` is a weighted sum over the prime powers up to x for a finite set of characters, with its main terms subtracted.

Let 0 < θ < 1 and la > 1. If for every bound there is a Y above it with `Gm x ≤ x^θ` for all x from Y to Y^la, then the L-functions of the characters of `Gm` have no zero with real part above θ. The proof applies this to every primitive character separately, with a set of characters that holds the powers of that character.
units.read: in full, ten lemmas by statement

units.states: The proof of `zero_free_all_of_green_v_win` uses la = 3/2. `core_gm` and `level_gm_le_on_family_scales` are implications with the conclusion `Gm x ≤ x^(1/2 + (eD + eL + 7)·ε)`, for every ε > 0. `core_gm` takes two conditions on a host and concludes it for all large x. `level_gm_le_on_family_scales` takes two conditions on a family and concludes it for the large x of a set of intervals that the family carries. `eD` and `eL` are two constants of the conditions. The statement `ChebyshevInequalityAtWindowScale` asks for them before ε, so the same two constants serve every small ε.

batches.title: Step 3, the wanted characters inside an auxiliary field

units.states: The condition `EAtH` on a host, one of the two conditions of `core_gm` in 2.3, has a field `kept`. It says that every character of `Gm`, the trivial one included, is the primitive character that induces some character of the host that is trivial on a subgroup `A0` and takes the value 1 at one element `iod` of the group. The code calls the characters of `Gm` kept, and it calls a character of the host kept when a character of `Gm` induces it.

The record of a host holds two primes q and d. The condition `WinPair` is a condition on two primes and the parameters Y and ε, and it does not mention a host. The proof applies it to the two primes of the host. It says that q ≡ 3 mod 8 and d ≡ 7 mod 16, that the logarithm of q lies between Y^(ε/5)/2 and Y^(ε/5), that the logarithm of d lies between Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)²/2 and Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)², and that q and every odd prime up to Y^(ε/5) divide d + 1.

`Bounded` is the set of the characters of the host that are trivial on `A0` and that either take the value 1 at `iod` and are not kept, or take the value −1 at `iod`. The condition `bdG` asks that every primitive character χ that induces one of them satisfies `‖gChi χ x‖ ≤ x^(1/2 + ε)`. `supplyOfAdmOf` supplies the condition under three premises, for the set of the powers of one primitive character, and `sigA_le` uses it.

Let 0 < ε < 1/52, let M be a modulus and let A ≥ 1 be an exponent that the caller chooses. For every large Y at least half of the candidate primes q, and for each of those at least half of the candidate primes d, give the following. Every character of modulus M, multiplied by the quadratic character of q, of d or of both, has a prime sum of at most y^(1/2 + ε/2) for every y from Y to Y^A. The same products with a real character whose modulus divides 8·M in place of the character of modulus M have no zero with real part above 1 − 1/400 up to a bounded height. `pair_exists` takes one such pair. `boundedTw` carries the bound to the set `Bounded` of 3.3 at the one point x, with the exponent 1/2 + ε, under a condition `TwistForm`. That condition says that every character of the host that is trivial on `A0` agrees with a power of one primitive character times the quadratic characters of q and of d, each to the exponent 0 or 1, and that its value at `iod` is −1 exactly when the exponent of d is 1.

`stage` says that the candidate primes that fail a condition form at most the share η of all candidates, for every η > 0 and every large Y, and that the set of candidates is not empty. The condition on a prime p is `Box` for the primitive character that induces ξ(n)·(n/p), for every ξ of a finite set of characters. In the proof a failing prime p is of one of two kinds. A primitive character of modulus f·p, with f at most a bound F, has a zero with real part above 1 − 1/400 and height at most F·U, or a truncated prime sum exceeds y^(1/2 + τ)/2 in absolute value for some y from Y to Y^K, for two parameters τ > 0 and K ≥ 1 of the statement.

For Q ≥ 3 at most a constant times Q^(1/4) primitive characters of modulus up to Q have a zero with real part above 1 − 1/400 and height up to Q, and with Q = F·U the same bound counts the candidate primes of the first kind of 3.5. For every large Y and every range that the condition `admitted` allows, the set of candidates holds at least U^(9/10) primes. The count of candidates takes the prime number theorem in progressions and a bound on real zeros as premises, and theorems of the project prove both.
units.read: `count_bad` in full, the others by statement

units.states: For every large Y and every range that `admitted` allows, for every y from Y to Y^K and every sequence of coefficients of absolute value at most 1, the squares of the truncated sums, added over the candidate primes, are at most a constant times y·log y times the number of primes. For every η > 0, every τ > 0 and every large Y, at most the share η of the primes then has a sum above y^(1/2 + τ)/2 at some y of that range.

Let n and n′ have a product below every candidate prime. The absolute value of the sum of (n/p)·(n′/p) over the candidate primes p of one residue class equals the absolute value of the sum of a real character (p/r) of p. Here r is the product of the primes outside the modulus of the class that divide n·n′ to an odd power, and r may be 1. Let A′ and B′ be any two exponents. For every odd squarefree r > 1 that is coprime to the modulus and at most Y^(A′), with one possible exception, the absolute value of that sum is at most Y^(−B′) times the number of primes, for every large Y and every range that `admitted` allows.

batches.title: Step 4, from the characters to an arithmetic quantity

units.states: `ASK` is a sum over the odd primes p up to a bound P, other than two primes `q1` and d of the host, whose Frobenius class lies outside a set `PhiSet` of classes. Each such prime adds 2·log p times a sum, over powers p^i, of the positive parts max(a/p^i − w, 0). Here a is a positive real number and w is a positive weight that depends on the class of p^i and, in the use of step 5, on an element of the group `H` and on a lift. A similar term with log d is added for the prime d. `MAIN` is the expression a·(log a − 1 − γ + L − W), where L is the value at one character of a function that the definition takes as data, and W is the mean of log w over `PhiSet`.

Let a > 0, let the weights w be positive on `PhiSet` and let P be at least a/w. Then `ASK − MAIN` equals `De`. `De` is one over the size of `PhiSet` times a double sum, over the classes g outside `PhiSet` and over all characters ψ of a finite abelian group `E0 × H`, of the conjugate of ψ(g) times a weight w times `GPsi` of ψ at a/w. `GPsi` has the form of the prime sum of one character, with the function of 4.1 in place of the logarithmic derivative, and the rows of this step call it the prime sum of ψ.

`core` takes a bound Err for `ASK − MAIN`, summed over a set `TT` and the m lifts, at every element of the subgroup `A0` of the group `H`. It takes a number g that is at most the mean over `TT` of the real part of a sum of prime sums, with values of the characters as coefficients, over the characters that are trivial on `A0`. It concludes nT·m·b·(δ2/2)·g ≤ Err + 2·nT·m·b/x. Here nT is the size of `TT`, b is a scale and δ2 is the ratio nT2/n, where nT2 is the size of a subset `T2` of `A0` and n is the size of `H`. In the proof one quantity, which holds no weight w and is the same for every lift, is at most `ASK − MAIN` of each lift plus 2·b/x, so the sum over the m lifts multiplies that quantity by m. A sum over the translates by `A0` then removes every character that is nontrivial on `A0`.

Let 0 ≤ C and 0 < ε. For every x beyond a threshold `ch_core` takes twelve conditions on sizes, windows and characters, and it takes the bound x^(Cε) times the bracket of 9.1 for `ASK − MAIN`, summed over `TT` and the m lifts, at every element of `A0`. It concludes that `GmA` is at most x^(1/2 + (C + 3)ε) plus `SigA`. `GmA` is a sum of the real parts of the prime sums of the kept characters, with weights of absolute value at most 1. `SigA` is the sum of the absolute values of the prime sums of the characters that are trivial on `A0` and not kept.

batches.title: Step 5, two bounds on one slope

units.states: `ch_top` works with a record of real numbers and real-valued functions whose first index u0 stands for an element of the group `H`. For every u0 it bounds `ASK − MAIN`, summed over `TT` and the m lifts, by x^(Cε) times the bracket of 9.1. It takes the eleven conditions `SizeData₂` on the record and four further premises. `IdentU` ties numbers of the record to the arithmetic data of step 4, `ErrWindows` and `LargeX` are conditions on sizes, and `BNBoundsU` bounds the two numbers `B0` and `Nc` of 9.1.

The condition `DIV` says for every index u0 of the record and every index u under it that a number `muCC` of u0 plus a number h of u, minus a third number of u0, is at most a main term plus errors. The main term is a sum over the top places. For each top place it holds m times the term of 7.4, minus the top weight a times the logarithm of a number T of u.

The condition `SlopeIneq` says for every u0 that a mean s of `muN` − h over the indices u, with positive weights, minus the logarithm of the number of indices and minus corrections, is at most `muCC`. It holds when three numbers of the record lie in stated ranges and a number `HH` is positive and at least s minus a number `muMinCC`. The condition `HHBound` gives `HH` those two properties and bounds it from above by a power of x times the scale b.

`each_unit_bound_statement` takes all eleven conditions of `SizeData₂` and concludes for every u0 that `ASK` is at most `Main` plus an explicit error. Two of the conditions bring in `ASK`. `QuotientSlopeBoundsWith` says that every `muN` is at least a quantity `Ga` of u0 plus further numbers of the record, and `LossBounds` says that `ASK` is at most `Ga` plus a loss. In the proof `s_lower5` derives from `DIV`, `QuotientSlopeBoundsWith`, `Count5`, `EComp5` and two further conditions that s is at least `Ga` + `muCC` minus two numbers. The identity of 5.5 turns one of the two into `Main` plus errors, and the other is an error. `Ga_bound5` adds `SlopeIneq`, by which s is at most `muCC` plus the logarithm of the number of indices and the corrections. The two bounds for s cancel `muCC`, and `Ga` is at most `Main` plus that logarithm and errors. By `LossBounds`, `ASK` is then at most `Main` plus errors.
units.read: `s_lower5` in full, `Ga_bound5` in full by a reading, the theorem by statement

units.states: Under the condition `HidaSetting` the record has a positive number w for each u0, each lift and each place. The condition `Count5` gives the logarithm of the number T of 5.2 three bounds. It is at least the sum over the lifts of the mean over the places of log(w·v/π), plus m times a further number, minus an error. It is at most a constant times m times a number of the record, and it varies between the indices u by at most a constant times log k. The number `Main` holds, for each lift and each top place, the expression a·(log a − 1 − `gam` + `LpL` − ℓ), where a is the top weight and ℓ is the mean over the places of log w. `gam` and `LpL` are fields of the record, and `IdentU` of 5.1 sets them to γ and to the real part of the value L of 4.1. `key_identity5` proves for positive v and w that the main term of 5.2, with the first of the three bounds in place of log T and with m times the further number times the sum of the top weights added back, equals `Main` plus an error.
units.read: definitions and the statement of the identity

batches.title: Step 6, the lattices and the chain of lifts

units.states: For a family a map assigns a datum to each element of a group, and the index u of the record runs over the words of that datum. `muCC` is the slope number of the dual of a lattice `RR` of the datum, and `muN` is the slope number of a further lattice, one for each word. `TieLocal` ties thirteen further numbers of the record to numbers of the datum.

The slope of a discrete lattice in a Euclidean space is minus the logarithm of its covolume, divided by its rank. For a lattice over a number field K the code's slope number is twice the slope of the lattice in a real inner product space, minus log 2, plus log \|d_K\| divided by the degree of K.

Each word has a linear map between two spaces that sends the lattice of the word into the dual of `RR`. The condition `WordFacts` requires that, when the map is not zero, the number h of the word is at least the height of the map. The height is the mean over the infinite places of the logarithm of the squared operator norm in chosen frames.

A pairing of each word factors through a chain of spaces. The spaces number 0 to m − 1 carry a unitary group of rank k + j(t + 1), for the number j of the space, together with two further groups. The last space carries a unitary group of rank k + m(t + 1) − 1, which the code extends to rank k + m(t + 1), with one further group. Here k and t are two natural numbers of the datum. Equalities of metrics and of operators tie the chain to m kernels. `rowsU_of_colPins_alt` proves for one word, under conditions on sizes and ties, that such a chain exists.

The chain has m − 1 matrices, under a condition that sets m to a natural number plus 2. The first m − 2 are kernels composed one after the other. The last matrix composes the last two kernels inside a finite weighted sum. A final linear map follows the matrices.

batches.title: Step 7, the bound for one lift

units.states: For every lift and every place, under a bundle `NumFacts` of 32 conditions, the sum of y·log y − y over the weights of the lift, minus the logarithm of a hook product, is at most a·log a − a at a top place and at most 0 elsewhere, plus an explicit error term. Here a is the top weight of the place. The same theorem bounds the absolute value of the sum of the weights minus k·w, and minus a at a top place, by a constant times w plus further terms. Here w is a number of the lift at the place, which the commentary calls the shift of the lift.
For every Young diagram the sum of the logarithms of the factorials of the row lengths is at most the logarithm of the hook product.
One of the 32 conditions of 7.1 says that the k numbers `uW` of a place and k − 1 numbers of the same place, the first k − 1 values of `sigPar`, interlace strictly.

The main term of 5.2 holds, for each lift and each top place, the term a·log a − a − a·`logOm`. `logOm` is γ + log(π/v) minus the real part of the logarithmic derivative at 1 of the L-function of the quadratic character modulo d, where v is a number of the host.

The slope inequality for the lattices of a datum follows from a general statement about a finite family of lattices with linear maps into one lattice. The proof applies it with the words of the datum as the family and the maps of 6.3 as the maps.

The general statement takes that each map sends its lattice into the target lattice with a height of at most a number h of that map. At one infinite place it takes for each map a matrix that is the product of a first factor and an isometry. On the rows of the target the product is the matrix of the map, and it may have further rows. A first factor may have more columns than its map, and the surplus over all maps is at most a quarter of the columns of the first factors. The statement takes three bounds on the first factors, with a positive weight for each map and a number `Dstar`. For two different maps the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the adjoint of one first factor times the other, times the two weights, is at most (1 + η0) times the product of their numbers of columns divided by `Dstar`. For one map the squared Hilbert-Schmidt distance of the weighted Gram matrix of its first factor from the identity is at most e0 times its number of columns. The number of rows is at most (1 + η1)·`Dstar`. The numbers η0, η1 and the square root of e0 are at most σ/2, for a number σ of at most 1/20. A bundle `LatNum` holds a number s that is at most the mean of the slope numbers minus the numbers h, and bounds for the largest and the smallest slopes. The statement concludes that s, minus the logarithm of the number of maps and minus a correction, is at most the slope number of the target lattice.

The proof of the general statement has two parts. The first turns the three bounds into two conditions on the products of the first factors with their isometries, for the whole family. One is on the trace of the square of the sum of the weighted products of each matrix with its adjoint, and one is on the sum of the distances of the Gram matrices from the identity. The second part, which the code calls the frame theorem, derives the inequality from those two conditions and the premises of 8.2 on the lattices.
units.read: the first part in full, the frame theorem at its top

units.states: The general statement also needs the numbers of columns of the first factors to add up to at least `Dstar`/σ. The proof of 8.1 applies the statement with σ = x^(−CH) and gets this from two conditions on the datum. The number of columns of the first factor of every word lies between `Dstar`/(C0·Γ²) and C0·`Dstar`/Γ², and the words number at least C0·Γ²·x^CH, for constants C0 and CH and a number Γ of the datum. A premise `DesignExists` says that families with these two conditions and further conditions exist.
units.read: the statements read and `word_count_bound_holds` in full, the theorems that prove `DesignExists` unread

units.states: Under the first condition of 8.4 and for large x a link gives the bounds of 8.2 for a second set of maps, one for each word, with η0, η1 and the square root of e0 at most exp(−x^(ε/8)). A condition `BlockReal_at` says that at one infinite place the matrix of the map of a word is the block on the rows of the target of the matrix of its second map times an isometry, up to a complex conjugation. A theorem proves that condition from a condition named `BesselId`. Two further theorems state the first two bounds for the matrices of the second maps, which are the first factors of 8.2.

The bound of 5.1 is x^(Cε) times the bracket nT·aE·(1 + m²/k) + m·(B + N), for a constant C and numbers nT, aE and k. The summand nT·aE carries no factor m. B stands for 2·n·m·b·x^ε and N stands for nT2·k·b·x^(2ε)/n², with nT2 and n as in 4.3, and a premise says that they bound two numbers `B0` and `Nc` of the record.
For a datum the number `B0` is a multiple of m, the product f·m·b·x^ε for a number f of the datum and b = exp(x^ε). The code calls it a budget.

`proposition_size_bound` proves the statement `GrowthSizeBound`, which is about a real number G. Its premise is nT·m·b·((nT2/n)/2)·(G − 4·x^(1/2 + ε)) ≤ Err + 2·nT·m·b/x, the conclusion of 4.3 with G − 4·x^(1/2 + ε) in the place of g, with Err at most x^(Cε) times the bracket of 9.1. Further premises put m between x^(1/2 − ε) and x^(1/2 + ε/2), bound the other numbers of the bracket, and ask that 3 ≤ x and 26 ≤ x^(3ε/8). The conclusion is G ≤ x^(1/2 + (C + 3)ε). The proof bounds the error by a multiple of nT·m·b and cancels that factor on both sides, which divides the error by a multiple of m.
units.read: by statement, the lines on the exponents read

units.states: `ch_core` applies 9.3 to the number G = `GmA` − `SigA` of 4.4. The conclusion of 4.4 follows, the exponent 1/2 + (C + 3)ε for the kept characters with the sum `SigA` of the other characters added.

`shape_closed_link_n_of_green` takes `Green` and concludes a statement `TopShapeAlt`, which has 53 binders of data and hypotheses before its conclusion. `goal_of_shape_of_hyps` fills 51 of them from the record `HypsAlt`, and `zero_free_all_of_green_v_win` fills the other two with `trivial`. The result is, for every small ε, a family that satisfies the condition `ChainTied`, under the premise that hosts exist. `supplyChi` gets the hosts from the bound of `VWin` for one primitive character.
units.read: in full, without the theorems they call

units.states: The premises of 1.4 are these. `Green` parametrises the cuspidal irreducible characters of the general linear groups over prime fields by irreducible polynomials. `VWin` bounds sums of lengths of Galois cohomology groups, weighted by the logarithms of primes, and it is derived from a statement that the code calls `Row`. `Row` says that Galois representations exist for the regular algebraic polarized cuspidal automorphic representations over CM fields. `HypsAlt` is a record of 46 fields, five of data and 41 conditions on the families. One of the conditions says that the chain of 6.4 exists for every word.
units.read: the statements of `VWin` and `Row` with their definitions, the proofs above them at their tops

batches.title: Entries 1 to 10 of the timeline of the note

units.paraphrase: A determinant in the manner of Stepanov.

On a curve with complex multiplication by a field K and a prime p inert in K, the p-th power of the invariant derivation vanishes modulo p, and the a-th derivative of a theta value at 0, divided by the a-th power of a period, is divisible by p to a power of about a/p + a/p^3.

An identity q·N = M^k + R for an exponential sum over a quadric of path shape, x1·x2 + … + x(k−1)·xk, where the sign of one side gives a proof of the Weil and Deligne bound from signs alone, and the wish that N be automorphic through a theta function on a sixfold cover of GL5.
Positivity of the Weil functional W on the indicator of a set S, obtained from a determinant and read as Stepanov's argument with multiplicity one, with a bootstrap.

The switch to the smoothed von Mangoldt sum, the sum of Λ(n)·(X/n − 1) over n ≤ X with the main terms X·log X − (1 + γ)·X subtracted, the sign in the explicit formula of Guinand and Weil, and a variance trick with a test function.
Positivity of W on the indicator of (0, 1] plus about X^η times the indicator of (0, 1/X] gives zero-freeness to the right of 1 − η.
Determinants for values of W that contain periods of Gan, Gross and Prasad, whose values 0 and 1 correspond to interlacing weights, or up to m weights that do not interlace.
Iterated theta lifts U(X0) → U(X1) → … → U(Xm) between totally definite unitary groups, each adding a block μ_j[t] to the representation, which win multiplicity m, with m about √X.

The norms and the level of the lifts, and the cancellation of the terms of order m, with a divisibility proved through the Chowla-Selberg formula, the Weyl dimension formula and the Siegel mass formula.
A sufficient lower bound for the divisibility of the m-fold iterated lift.

batches.title: Entries 11 to 20 of the timeline of the note

units.paraphrase: An Iwasawa tower, by analogy with a pigeonhole argument on the extension F_(q^n) over F_q.
A seesaw identity in the manner of Rallis. The period of the iterated lift is a Bessel period that does not depend on the Hecke characters.
The slope inequality of Bost.
The exact cost of each lift, which shows that the method alone would stop at the exponent 2/3, and the need for a main term and for a division.
An integral structure glued together across Hecke characters, which acts as a greatest common divisor and gives an extra averaging.
A relative trace formula, reduced by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to a bound on the norm of a projected Poincaré series, and approximate orthogonality of the columns of the integral structure.
For the classes in H^1(o_E[1/ℓ], Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ(−e)) that twisting does not remove, a substantial weakening of the Vandiver conjecture.
The computation of covolumes, of the index of theta series, and of congruences between lifts and forms.
The exact choice of the Iwasawa tower, which uses a result of Behrend.
The conclusion, the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
